stem:
What happens when this runs under CPython 3.13?

```python
def double(x: int) -> int:
    return x * 2

print(double("ab"))
```

options.text: It prints `abab`
options.why: Python does not enforce annotations, so the string is simply multiplied by 2.

options.text: It raises `TypeError` before the call
options.why: No check happens at call time; annotations are not runtime contracts.

options.text: It prints `4`, after coercing the string
options.why: Python never coerces arguments to match their annotations.

options.text: It fails at definition time with `SyntaxError`
options.why: The annotation syntax is valid; nothing is wrong with the definition.

explanation: Annotations are metadata. CPython stores them in `double.__annotations__` but never checks arguments against them, so `"ab" * 2` runs and returns `'abab'`. Only a static checker such as mypy or pyright (or a runtime validator such as Pydantic) would flag the call.

stem: True or false: calling a function with an argument that does not match its type annotation raises a `TypeError` at runtime.

options.text: True
options.why: There is no runtime enforcement; the call proceeds with whatever value was passed.

options.text: False
options.why: Correct: annotations are not checked by the interpreter, only by external tools.

explanation: False. CPython ignores annotations when calling functions. They are available for tools (`__annotations__`, `typing.get_type_hints`) and static checkers, and libraries like Pydantic or beartype can opt into runtime checks, but the interpreter itself does not.

stem: A function is defined as `def f(x: int) -> str: ...`. Type the name of the attribute on `f` that holds the dictionary `{'x': int, 'return': str}`.
explanation: Function annotations are stored in the `__annotations__` dictionary, keyed by parameter name plus `'return'`. Prefer `typing.get_type_hints(f)` (or `annotationlib.get_annotations` in 3.14) when you need string annotations resolved.

stem: Which annotation is exactly equivalent to `Optional[int]`?

options.text: `int | None`
options.why: Both spell the union of `int` and `None`, and they compare equal at runtime.

options.text: `int | object`
options.why: That union is just `object`, which accepts every value, not only ints and None.

options.text: `Union[int]`
options.why: A one-member union collapses to `int`; it does not include None.

options.text: `Any`
options.why: `Any` turns off checking entirely rather than allowing exactly int or None.

explanation: `Optional[X]` is shorthand for `Union[X, None]`, and since Python 3.10 the same union can be written `X | None`. At runtime `typing.Optional[int] == (int | None)` is `True`. Note that `Optional` means "may be None", not "optional argument": a parameter still needs a default to be omittable.

stem: Match each special type with what it means to a type checker.

options.text: Every operation is allowed and checking is switched off
options.why: This describes `Any`.

options.text: Any value fits, but only methods common to all objects can be used
options.why: This describes `object`.

options.text: No value has this type; used for code that cannot be reached
options.why: This describes `Never`.

options.text: The only allowed value is `None`
options.why: This describes `None` used as a type.

explanation: `Any` is the escape hatch: it is compatible with everything in both directions, so errors silently disappear. `object` is the top type: anything can be assigned to it, but you can only use operations every object supports. `Never` (or `NoReturn`) is the bottom type with no values, used for functions that never return and for exhaustiveness checks. `None` in an annotation means the single value `None`.

stem:
What happens with this module?

```python
from typing import Final

MAX: Final = 3
MAX = 4
print(MAX)
```

options.text: mypy reports an error, but at runtime it prints `4`
options.why: The checker forbids rebinding; the interpreter does not know about `Final`.

options.text: It raises `AttributeError` on the second assignment
options.why: Module globals have no runtime protection from `Final`.

options.text: It prints `3`, because the second assignment is ignored
options.why: Python executes every assignment; nothing is silently skipped.

options.text: Both mypy and Python accept it, since `Final` only affects classes
options.why: `Final` applies to module-level names too, and mypy rejects the rebinding.

explanation: `Final` is enforced only by type checkers. mypy reports `Cannot assign to final name "MAX"`, but CPython happily rebinds the name and prints 4. For a real runtime constant you would need a different mechanism (a property, an enum or a frozen dataclass).

stem: Given `Mode = Literal["r", "w"]` and `def open_file(path: str, mode: Mode) -> None: ...`, which calls does mypy accept? (Choose two.)

options.text: `open_file("a.txt", "r")`
options.why: "r" is one of the two allowed literal values.

options.text: `open_file("a.txt", "w")`
options.why: "w" is the other allowed literal value.

options.text: `open_file("a.txt", "rw")`
options.why: "rw" is not in the literal set, so mypy rejects it.

options.text: `open_file("a.txt", "R")`
options.why: Literal matching is exact and case-sensitive.

options.text: `m: str = "r"; open_file("a.txt", m)`
options.why: `m` is typed as `str`, which is wider than `Literal["r", "w"]`.

explanation: `Literal` types accept only the exact listed values. A plain `str` variable is rejected even if its value happens to be "r", because the checker only knows it is some string; annotate it as `Mode` or narrow it first. Literal matching is case-sensitive and exact.

stem:
What does this print?

```python
from typing import TypedDict

class Movie(TypedDict):
    title: str

m = Movie(title=1)
print(type(m).__name__, m)
```

options.text: `dict {'title': 1}`
options.why: The class call returns an ordinary dict, and the int is stored unchanged.

options.text: `Movie {'title': 1}`
options.why: There is no `Movie` instance type at runtime; the object is a dict.

options.text: It raises `TypeError` because `title` must be a `str`
options.why: TypedDict performs no runtime type checks.

options.text: `dict {'title': '1'}`
options.why: Nothing converts the value; the int 1 is stored as is.

explanation: A `TypedDict` is erased at runtime: calling `Movie(...)` just builds a plain `dict`, and no field types are checked. A static checker would flag `title=1`; for runtime validation you need something like Pydantic or a `TypeAdapter`.

stem:
Why does mypy reject the call on the last line?

```python
def mean(xs: list[float]) -> float:
    return sum(xs) / len(xs)

ints: list[int] = [1, 2, 3]
mean(ints)
```

options.text: `list` is invariant; a read-only `Sequence[float]` would accept it
options.why: Invariance protects callers from the callee inserting floats into their int list.

options.text: `int` is not compatible with `float`, so no int container ever matches
options.why: mypy does treat `int` as compatible with `float`; the problem is the mutable container.

options.text: Literal lists infer as `list[Literal[1, 2, 3]]`, which is too narrow
options.why: `ints` is explicitly annotated `list[int]`; literals play no part here.

options.text: `sum` returns `int` for int lists, so the return type is wrong
options.why: The return expression is fine; the error is on the argument.

explanation: mypy reports `"list" is invariant` and suggests `Sequence`. If `list[int]` were accepted as `list[float]`, `mean` could legally append `0.5` to it, corrupting a list the caller still treats as ints. Since `mean` only reads, annotate it with the covariant `Sequence[float]` (or `Iterable[float]`).

stem: A variable is declared `d: dict[str, int] = {}`. Which parameter annotations accept `d` under mypy? (Choose two.)

options.text: `Mapping[str, float]`
options.why: Mapping is read-only and covariant in its value type.

options.text: `dict[str, int]`
options.why: An exact match is always accepted.

options.text: `dict[str, float]`
options.why: dict is invariant in its value type, so int and float values do not mix.

options.text: `dict[str, object]`
options.why: Even `object` is rejected: the callee could insert a string.

options.text: `MutableMapping[str, float]`
options.why: Mutable mappings are invariant, just like dict.

explanation: `dict` and `MutableMapping` are invariant in their value type because callees could write into them, so `dict[str, float]`, `dict[str, object]` and `MutableMapping[str, float]` are all rejected. The read-only `Mapping` is covariant in its value, so `Mapping[str, float]` accepts a `dict[str, int]`. The exact type always matches.
reference: Python docs: collections.abc.Mapping; mypy docs: variance

stem:
mypy reports this for the line `items = []` at module level:

```
error: Need type annotation for "items" (hint: "items: list[<type>] = ...")  [???]
```

Type the error code shown in the brackets.
explanation: mypy cannot infer an element type from an empty literal with no later usage in scope, so it reports `[var-annotated]`. Fix it with `items: list[str] = []`. pyright instead infers `list[Unknown]` and reports it only in strict mode, one of several inference differences between the checkers.

stem:
What does mypy (default settings) say about this function?

```python
def greet(name: str = None) -> str:
    return f"Hi {name}"
```

options.text: Error: a `None` default needs the type `str | None`
options.why: Implicit Optional is no longer inferred, so `None` is incompatible with `str`.

options.text: Accepted: a `None` default makes the parameter `Optional[str]`
options.why: That was old implicit-Optional behaviour, now disabled by default.

options.text: Error: f-strings cannot interpolate optional values
options.why: Interpolating any object into an f-string is fine; the error is the default.

options.text: Accepted, because annotations on defaults are ignored
options.why: mypy checks a default value against the parameter type.

explanation: PEP 484 originally allowed "implicit Optional", treating `str = None` as `Optional[str]`. It was removed from the spec, and mypy has defaulted to `no_implicit_optional=True` since 0.990, so the default is reported as incompatible. Write `name: str | None = None` and handle the None case.

stem:
Which statement about this code is correct?

```python
from typing import NewType

UserId = NewType("UserId", int)

def load(uid: UserId) -> None: ...

load(5)            # line 1
load(UserId(5))    # line 2
print(type(UserId(5)))
```

options.text: mypy rejects line 1 only, and the print shows `<class 'int'>`
options.why: The distinction exists at type-check time; at runtime the value is a plain int.

options.text: mypy rejects line 1 only, and the print shows `<class 'UserId'>`
options.why: NewType does not create a runtime class; the object stays an int.

options.text: mypy accepts both lines, since `UserId` is just an alias for `int`
options.why: That describes a type alias. NewType is a distinct subtype, so plain ints are rejected.

options.text: mypy rejects both lines, since `UserId(5)` still has type `int`
options.why: Calling `UserId(...)` is how you produce a value of the new type.

explanation: `NewType` creates a distinct type for the checker only. mypy rejects passing a plain `int` (line 1) and accepts `UserId(5)` (line 2). At runtime `UserId` is an identity function, so `UserId(5)` is just the int `5` and `type(...)` prints `<class 'int'>`. Arithmetic like `UserId(5) + 1` returns plain `int`.

stem:
Running this file with CPython 3.13 (no `__future__` import), what happens?

```python
def handle(event: Event) -> None:
    ...

class Event:
    pass
```

options.text: `NameError` as soon as the `def` statement executes
options.why: 3.13 evaluates function annotations at definition time.

options.text: It runs fine, because annotations are only evaluated by type checkers
options.why: That is 3.14 behaviour (PEP 649); 3.13 still evaluates them eagerly.

options.text: `NameError` only when `handle` is first called
options.why: Annotations are evaluated with the `def`, not at call time.

options.text: `SyntaxError`, because forward references must be quoted
options.why: Unquoted forward references are syntactically valid; the failure is a NameError.

explanation: In 3.13 annotations on functions are evaluated eagerly when the `def` statement runs, and `Event` is not defined yet, so the module fails with `NameError`. Fixes are quoting the annotation (`"Event"`), `from __future__ import annotations`, or moving the class first. Python 3.14 implements PEP 649, which evaluates annotations lazily, so this exact code works there.
reference: PEP 649; Python docs: Annotations best practices

stem:
What does this print under CPython 3.13?

```python
from __future__ import annotations

def f(x: int, y: Undefined) -> list[int]: ...

print(f.__annotations__)
```

options.text: `{'x': 'int', 'y': 'Undefined', 'return': 'list[int]'}`
options.why: Postponed evaluation keeps the annotation source text as strings.

options.text: `{'x': <class 'int'>, 'y': None, 'return': list[int]}`
options.why: Nothing is evaluated, so there are no class objects or None placeholders.

options.text: It raises `NameError` for `Undefined` at definition time
options.why: The future import prevents evaluation, so the undefined name is never looked up.

options.text: `{}`, because postponed annotations are not stored at all
options.why: They are stored, just as strings.

explanation: The `__future__` import (PEP 563) stores every annotation as a string instead of evaluating it, so the undefined name causes no error and the dict holds strings. Resolving them later with `typing.get_type_hints(f)` would raise `NameError` for `Undefined`. Python 3.14 makes annotations lazy by default (PEP 649) but keeps this import working.

stem:
Using the PEP 695 syntax from Python 3.12, what does `first.__type_params__` contain at runtime?

```python
def first[T](xs: list[T]) -> T:
    return xs[0]
```

options.text: A one-item tuple holding a `TypeVar` named `T`
options.why: PEP 695 creates the TypeVar automatically and records it on the function.

options.text: An empty tuple, because type parameters are erased at runtime
options.why: They are introspectable objects; only argument checking is absent.

options.text: `('T',)`, the parameter name as a string
options.why: A real `typing.TypeVar` object is stored, not a string.

options.text: `(list,)`, the type found in the annotation
options.why: The tuple holds the declared type variables, not types from the signature.

explanation: The `[T]` clause creates an implicit `TypeVar` named `T`, scoped to the function, and stores it in `__type_params__` as `(T,)`. You no longer need a module-level `T = TypeVar("T")`. A checker infers `T` from each call, so `first([1, 2])` has type `int`.

stem: Order these types from the narrowest (fewest values) to the widest (most values), so that each is assignable to every type after it.

options.text: `Literal[1]`
options.why: Exactly one value.

options.text: `int`
options.why: All integers, including 1.

options.text: `int | str`
options.why: All ints plus all strings.

options.text: `object`
options.why: Every Python value.

explanation: `Literal[1]` has one value; every `int` includes it; `int | str` adds all strings; and `object` is the top type that every value belongs to. Thinking of types as sets of values makes assignability questions much easier.
reference: Python typing spec: Type system concepts

stem: True or false: with `@dataclass class P: x: int`, the call `P("not an int")` raises a `TypeError`.

options.text: True
options.why: Dataclasses do not check field types at runtime.

options.text: False
options.why: Correct: the instance is created with the string stored in `x`.

explanation: False. `@dataclass` reads annotations only to decide which fields to generate; it does not validate values. `P("not an int")` succeeds and prints `P(x='not an int')`. Use Pydantic, attrs validators or `__post_init__` checks if you need validation.

stem:
What does mypy report for this code?

```python
from typing import ClassVar

class Config:
    count: ClassVar[int] = 0

c = Config()
c.count = 5
```

options.text: An error: the class variable is assigned via an instance
options.why: ClassVar attributes must be set on the class itself.

options.text: No error: assigning creates a normal instance attribute
options.why: That is the runtime effect, but mypy flags it as a likely mistake.

options.text: An error: `ClassVar` attributes cannot have default values
options.why: Class variables usually do have a value; the problem is the instance assignment.

options.text: No error, because `ClassVar` only matters for dataclasses
options.why: mypy enforces ClassVar in every class, not just dataclasses.

explanation: `ClassVar` declares an attribute that belongs to the class, so mypy reports `Cannot assign to class variable "count" via instance`. At runtime the assignment would create an instance attribute that shadows the class one, which is usually a bug. Write `Config.count = 5` to change the shared value.

options.text: Line A is `int | str`, line B is `int`
options.why: TypeGuard narrows only when true; TypeIs also narrows when false.

options.text: Line A is `int`, line B is `int`
options.why: TypeGuard gives no information when the guard returns False.

options.text: Line A is `int | str`, line B is `int | str`
options.why: TypeIs does narrow the negative branch.

options.text: Line A is `object`, line B is `int`
options.why: Narrowing starts from the declared `int | str`, not from the guard's parameter type.

explanation: A `TypeGuard` narrows only in the positive branch; in the negative branch the type is unchanged (`int | str`). `TypeIs` (PEP 742, Python 3.13) narrows both ways like `isinstance`, so the negative branch becomes `int`. Prefer `TypeIs` for ordinary predicates; keep `TypeGuard` for cases where the narrowed type is not a subtype of the input.

stem: Which of these predicate signatures does mypy accept without an error? (Choose two.)

options.text: `def f(x: list[object]) -> TypeGuard[list[str]]: ...`
options.why: TypeGuard allows narrowing to a type that is not a subtype of the input.

options.text: `def f(x: object) -> TypeIs[str]: ...`
options.why: `str` is a subtype of `object`, as TypeIs requires.

options.text: `def f(x: list[object]) -> TypeIs[list[str]]: ...`
options.why: list is invariant, so `list[str]` is not a subtype of `list[object]`.

options.text: `def f(x: str) -> TypeIs[int]: ...`
options.why: `int` is not a subtype of `str`, so the narrowing is rejected.

options.text: `def f(x: object) -> TypeIs: ...`
options.why: TypeIs needs a type argument, such as `TypeIs[str]`.

explanation: `TypeIs[T]` requires the narrowed type to be a subtype of the parameter type, because it narrows both branches. `list[str]` is not a subtype of `list[object]` (lists are invariant) and `int` is not a subtype of `str`, so both TypeIs versions fail with `narrowed-type-not-subtype`. `TypeGuard` has no such rule, which is why it still exists for cases like `list[object]` to `list[str]`.

options.text: An error on the last line: argument 1 must be an `int`
options.why: ParamSpec keeps `add`'s parameters, so the wrong argument type is caught.

options.text: No error, because a decorated function's parameters become `*Any, **Any`
options.why: That happens with `Callable[..., Any]`, not with ParamSpec.

options.text: An error in `wrapper`: `P.args` must be paired with an explicit return type
options.why: The wrapper is typed correctly; the only error is the call.

options.text: No error, because `functools.wraps` hides the signature from mypy
options.why: `wraps` copies metadata at runtime and does not erase the static type.

explanation: `ParamSpec` captures the decorated function's full parameter list, so `logged(add)` has the type `def (x: int, y: int) -> int`, and the bad call is reported: `Argument 1 to "add" has incompatible type "str"; expected "int"`. Decorators typed as `Callable[..., Any]` lose that information.

stem:
This decorator is typed loosely. What type does mypy reveal for `sub`, and is the bad call reported?

```python
from typing import Any, Callable

def loose(fn: Callable[..., Any]) -> Callable[..., Any]:
    return fn

@loose
def sub(x: int, y: int) -> int:
    return x - y

reveal_type(sub)
sub("a", 1)
```

options.text: `def (*Any, **Any) -> Any`, and the call is not reported
options.why: The decorator's return type erases the parameters and the return type.

options.text: `def (x: int, y: int) -> int`, and the call is reported
options.why: mypy uses the decorator's declared return type, not the original function's.

options.text: `Callable[..., int]`, and the call is reported
options.why: The return type is `Any` as well, and `...` accepts any arguments.

options.text: `Any`, and mypy reports that `sub` is untyped
options.why: It reveals a callable type, and no error is emitted.

explanation: The return annotation `Callable[..., Any]` is all mypy knows about the decorated name, so it reveals `def (*Any, **Any) -> Any` and accepts any arguments. That is how a careless decorator silently switches off checking for every function it touches. Typing it with `ParamSpec` and `TypeVar` preserves the signature.

options.text: `get_user(42)`
options.why: The decorator supplies `db`, leaving only `uid: int`.

options.text: `get_user("db-conn", 42)`
options.why: The decorated signature no longer has a `db` parameter, so this is too many arguments.

options.text: `get_user(db="db-conn", uid=42)`
options.why: There is no `db` parameter left to pass by keyword.

options.text: `get_user()`
options.why: `uid` is still required, since only the first parameter is supplied.

explanation: `Concatenate[str, P]` says the wrapped function takes a `str` first, followed by the parameters captured in `P`. The decorator injects that first argument itself and returns `Callable[P, R]`, so the decorated function is revealed as `def (uid: int) -> str`. Passing the connection again is "Too many arguments".

stem: A function is declared `def run(cb: Callable[[int], object]) -> None: ...`. Which callbacks does mypy accept? (Choose two.)

options.text: `def a(x: object) -> int: ...`
options.why: Accepting `object` is wider than `int`, which is safe for a parameter.

options.text: `def c(x: int) -> str: ...`
options.why: Exact parameter, and any return type fits `object`.

options.text: `def b(x: bool) -> None: ...`
options.why: `bool` is narrower than `int`; the callback could receive 5.

options.text: `def d(x: str) -> None: ...`
options.why: A `str` parameter cannot accept the ints that `run` passes.

options.text: `def e() -> None: ...`
options.why: `run` calls the callback with one argument, which `e` does not accept.

explanation: Callable types are contravariant in their parameters and covariant in their return type. A callback may accept a wider parameter (`object` handles any int) and return anything, since `object` is the declared return. A callback that only accepts `bool` or `str` cannot handle every int, and a zero-argument function cannot be called with one.
reference: mypy docs: Callable types and variance

options.text: An error saying `Literal['tri']` was passed where `Never` is expected
options.why: The unhandled case reaches `assert_never` and is reported.

options.text: No error: `assert_never` only fails at runtime
options.why: It is designed to produce a static error when a case is missing.

options.text: An error saying the function is missing a `return` statement
options.why: mypy treats `assert_never` as never returning, so no return is needed.

options.text: An error saying `==` cannot compare a Literal with a str
options.why: Comparing literal types with `==` is how narrowing works here.

explanation: After the two checks, mypy narrows `s` to `Literal['tri']` in the `else` branch. `assert_never` accepts only `Never`, so mypy reports `Argument 1 to "assert_never" has incompatible type "Literal['tri']"; expected "Never"`. That error is the point: it turns a forgotten case into a type error, and it disappears once "tri" is handled.

options.text: Yes: `Self` makes `set` return `SqlBuilder` here
options.why: Self binds to the class of the object the method is called on.

options.text: No: `set` returns `Builder`, which has no `where`
options.why: That would be true with `-> Builder`, not with `Self`.

options.text: No: `Self` cannot be used in a class that is subclassed
options.why: Subclassing is exactly the case `Self` is designed for.

options.text: Yes, but only because `where` is not type-checked
options.why: The chain is fully checked and resolves correctly to `SqlBuilder`.

explanation: `Self` is bound to the type of the receiver, so `SqlBuilder().set(1)` is revealed as `SqlBuilder` and `.where()` type-checks. Had `set` been annotated `-> "Builder"`, the chained call would fail with `"Builder" has no attribute "where"`. `Self` (3.11+) replaces the older bound-TypeVar pattern.

stem: Which statements about `Annotated[int, "meta"]` are true? (Choose two.)

options.text: `get_type_hints()` returns plain `int` unless `include_extras=True` is passed
options.why: By default the metadata is stripped from resolved hints.

options.text: To a static checker, the annotation means exactly `int`
options.why: Metadata does not change the type the checker sees.

options.text: Python checks at runtime that the value matches `"meta"`
options.why: Python never interprets the metadata; libraries may choose to.

options.text: The metadata must itself be a type, such as a class
options.why: Any object may be used as metadata.

options.text: mypy reports an error unless the metadata is registered
options.why: There is no registration step; arbitrary metadata is allowed.

explanation: `Annotated[T, x]` is just `T` to a type checker; the extra metadata is ignored statically but kept for runtime consumers such as Pydantic, FastAPI or SQLAlchemy. `typing.get_type_hints()` strips the metadata unless you pass `include_extras=True`. Python does not validate the metadata, and it does not need to be a type.

options.text: `m1`, because `title` is still required
options.why: Required overrides `total=False` for that key.

options.text: `m2`, because `year` is missing
options.why: `total=False` makes `year` optional.

options.text: None of them, because `total=False` makes every key optional
options.why: The `Required` marker makes `title` an exception.

options.text: `m3`, because `Required` keys cannot be mixed with optional ones
options.why: Mixing required and optional keys is the purpose of Required and NotRequired.

explanation: `total=False` makes keys optional by default, but `Required[...]` overrides that for `title`. So `m1` is rejected with `Missing key "title"`, while `m2` (no `year`) and `m3` are fine. `NotRequired[...]` is the mirror image, for marking individual keys optional in a total TypedDict.

stem:
What type does mypy reveal for `s`?

```python
from typing import Generator

def worker() -> Generator[int, str, bool]:
    s = yield 1
    reveal_type(s)
    return True
```

options.text: `str`
options.why: The second type argument is the type of values sent into the generator.

options.text: `int`
options.why: `int` is what the generator yields, not what `yield` evaluates to.

options.text: `bool`
options.why: `bool` is the return type, delivered when the generator finishes.

options.text: `None`
options.why: That would be true for `Generator[int, None, ...]`, where nothing is sent.

explanation: `Generator[YieldType, SendType, ReturnType]`: the generator yields ints, receives strings through `.send()`, and returns a bool (the value carried by `StopIteration` and by `yield from`). The value of a `yield` expression is whatever was sent, so `s` is `str`. If you only yield, `Iterator[int]` is a simpler annotation.

stem: Match each type variable declaration with how mypy solves it.

options.text: Any type at all
options.why: Unbounded TypeVar.

options.text: Any subtype of `Sized`, solved to the most specific match
options.why: Bounded TypeVar.

options.text: Exactly `str` or exactly `bytes`, never a mix
options.why: Constrained TypeVar.

options.text: `Box[bool]` may be used where `Box[int]` is expected
options.why: Covariant TypeVar on a generic class.

explanation: An unbounded TypeVar can be any type. A `bound=` TypeVar can be any subtype of the bound and is solved to the most specific type that fits. A constrained TypeVar must be exactly one of the listed types (`AnyStr` is `TypeVar("AnyStr", str, bytes)`). `covariant=True` affects how the generic class built with it relates to other instances, not what values it accepts.

options.text: True
options.why: The runtime check only looks for an attribute named `close`.

options.text: False
options.why: No signature or callability check is performed, so `close = 42` still matches.

explanation: True. A `runtime_checkable` protocol's `isinstance` check only tests that each member exists (`hasattr`); it does not check that `close` is callable or has the right signature. So an `int` attribute named `close` passes. Static checkers would reject `F` as a `Closer`; at runtime, treat these checks as a cheap duck-typing test.

mypy reports this for the line below:

```python
total: int = "seven"  # type: ignore[arg-type]
```

```
error: Incompatible types in assignment (expression has type "str", variable has type "int")  [assignment]
note: Error code "assignment" not covered by "type: ignore[arg-type]" comment
```

Type the error code that should go in the brackets to silence this error.
explanation: A bracketed `# type: ignore[code]` silences only the listed codes, so the wrong code leaves the error visible (and with `--warn-unused-ignores` mypy also flags the useless ignore). The error is `[assignment]`. Scoped ignores are better than bare `# type: ignore` because they don't hide unrelated new errors.

stem:
What does mypy report for the first call?

```python
from typing import AnyStr

def concat(a: AnyStr, b: AnyStr) -> AnyStr:
    return a + b

concat(b"a", "b")
reveal_type(concat("a", "b"))
```

options.text: An error: `AnyStr` cannot be solved to `Sequence[object]`
options.why: A constrained TypeVar must be exactly `str` or exactly `bytes` for every argument.

options.text: No error: `AnyStr` is solved to `str | bytes`
options.why: Constrained TypeVars are never solved to a union of their constraints.

options.text: No error: `bytes` is accepted wherever `str` is expected
options.why: `bytes` and `str` are unrelated types in Python 3.

options.text: An error: `+` is not defined for `AnyStr` operands inside the body
options.why: Inside the function `a + b` checks fine for each constraint separately.

explanation: `AnyStr` is a constrained TypeVar (`str` or `bytes`). Both arguments must solve it to the same constraint, and mixing them makes mypy try their join, reporting `Value of type variable "AnyStr" of "concat" cannot be "Sequence[object]"`. The second call solves cleanly to `str`. A bounded TypeVar or a union would have hidden this mistake.

stem:
What does mypy reveal, and is there an error?

```python
from typing import Sized

def longest[T: Sized](a: T, b: T) -> T:
    return a if len(a) >= len(b) else b

reveal_type(longest([1], "ab"))
```

options.text: No error; it reveals `typing.Sequence[object]`
options.why: mypy joins the two argument types and checks the join against the bound.

options.text: An error: both arguments must have the same type `T`
options.why: A bounded TypeVar can be solved to a common supertype.

options.text: No error; it reveals `list[int] | str`
options.why: mypy uses the join rather than a union for TypeVar solutions.

options.text: No error; it reveals `Sized`
options.why: mypy picks the most specific common type, which is narrower than the bound.

explanation: With a bound (not constraints), mypy solves `T` from both arguments by joining `list[int]` and `str`. Their join is `Sequence[object]`, which satisfies the `Sized` bound, so there is no error and the result type is `Sequence[object]`. Many people expect either an error or `list[int] | str`; if you need both arguments to have the same type, use separate overloads or constraints.

options.text: Line 2 only: the public mutable attribute makes `MBox` invariant
options.why: Writable attributes force invariance; read-only use allows covariance.

options.text: Line 1 only, because PEP 695 classes are always invariant
options.why: PEP 695 classes infer variance; they are not always invariant.

options.text: Both lines, because `bool` and `int` are different types
options.why: `bool` is a subtype of `int`, so covariance makes line 1 valid.

options.text: Neither line, because variance is ignored for user-defined classes
options.why: mypy checks variance for user generics, and it rejects line 2.

explanation: With PEP 695 syntax the checker infers variance from usage. In `Box`, `T` appears only in output positions (returned from `get`, stored privately), so `Box` is covariant and `Box[bool]` fits `Box[int]`. In `MBox`, `T` is the type of a public mutable attribute, which can be both read and written, so it is invariant and line 2 is rejected.

What happens at runtime?

```python
from typing import Protocol, runtime_checkable

@runtime_checkable
class HasName(Protocol):
    name: str

class N:
    name = "x"

print(isinstance(N(), HasName))
print(issubclass(N, HasName))
```

options.text: It prints `True`, then `issubclass` raises `TypeError`
options.why: `issubclass` is unsupported for protocols that have data members.

options.text: It prints `True` twice
options.why: `issubclass` refuses protocols with non-method members.

options.text: `isinstance` raises `TypeError`, since only methods can be checked
options.why: `isinstance` handles data members by checking that the attribute exists.

options.text: It prints `False` twice, since `name` is a class attribute
options.why: A class attribute is visible on instances, so `isinstance` returns True.

explanation: For a runtime_checkable protocol with a data member, `isinstance` works (it checks for the attribute, printing `True`), but `issubclass` raises `TypeError: Protocols with non-method members don't support issubclass()`. Instance attributes might be set in `__init__`, so a class-level check can't be reliable.

Using Pydantic v2 with default (lax) settings:

```python
from pydantic import BaseModel, ConfigDict

class U(BaseModel):
    age: int
    tags: list[str] = []

class S(BaseModel):
    model_config = ConfigDict(strict=True)
    age: int
```

Which statements are true? (Choose three.)

options.text: `U(age="1").age` is the int `1`
options.why: Lax mode parses numeric strings into ints.

options.text: `U(age="1.5")` raises `ValidationError`
options.why: A string with a fractional part is not a valid int.

options.text: `U(age=1.0).age` is the int `1`
options.why: A float with no fractional part is accepted in lax mode.

options.text: `S(age="1")` succeeds, since strict mode only affects floats
options.why: Strict mode rejects the string with an `int_type` error.

options.text: `U.model_construct(age="nope")` raises `ValidationError`
options.why: `model_construct` bypasses validation entirely.

options.text: Appending to `tags` on one instance changes it on another
options.why: Pydantic copies mutable defaults for each instance.

explanation: Lax mode coerces "1" and the float 1.0 (no fractional part) to `int`, but rejects "1.5" with an `int_parsing` error. Strict mode refuses the string with `int_type`. `model_construct` skips validation entirely, so it happily stores "nope". Pydantic copies mutable defaults per instance, so the classic shared-list bug does not occur.
reference: Pydantic docs: Conversion table and strict mode

stem: A Pydantic v2 model has an `int` field with both a `mode="before"` and a `mode="after"` field validator. When `V(n="5")` is called, put these steps in the order they happen.

options.text: The `before` validator runs on the raw string `"5"`
options.why: First: it sees the untouched input.

options.text: Core validation parses `"5"` into the int `5`
options.why: Second: the type is enforced.

options.text: The `after` validator runs on the int `5`
options.why: Third: it sees the validated value.

options.text: The model instance is created with `n = 5`
options.why: Last: the instance holds the final value.

explanation: `before` validators receive the raw input (here the string "5"), then Pydantic's core validation parses it into an int, then `after` validators receive the already-converted value, and finally the model instance is built. A logging validator shows `('before', 'str')` then `('after', 'int')`. Put sanitising logic in `before` and business rules in `after`.

options.text: An `int` matches both overloads, which promise different return types
options.why: Overlapping inputs with incompatible returns make the overloads unsafe.

options.text: The implementation must repeat the `@overload` decorator
options.why: The implementation must not be decorated with `@overload`.

options.text: Overloads may not use `object` as a parameter type
options.why: `object` is allowed; the issue is the overlap with `int`.

options.text: The implementation returns `1`, which doesn't match the second overload
options.why: mypy does not check the body against each overload's return type.

explanation: mypy reports `Overloaded function signatures 1 and 2 overlap with incompatible return types`. An `int` argument matches both signatures, but they promise different returns (`int` vs `str`). That is unsafe: an int passed through a variable typed `object` would match the second overload and be typed `str`, even though the int overload says it returns `int`. Narrow the second overload (for example `x: str`) so the inputs don't overlap.

With `mypy --warn-unreachable`, what is reported?

```python
from typing import NoReturn

def fail(msg: str) -> NoReturn:
    raise RuntimeError(msg)

def check(x: int) -> int:
    if x < 0:
        fail("negative")
        print("cleanup")
    return x
```

options.text: `print("cleanup")` is reported as unreachable
options.why: After a NoReturn call, mypy knows the next statement can never run.

options.text: An error that `fail` is missing a return statement
options.why: A function that always raises satisfies NoReturn.

options.text: An error that `check` may return `None` when `x < 0`
options.why: The negative branch never falls through, so no implicit None return exists.

options.text: Nothing: `--warn-unreachable` ignores function calls
options.why: mypy uses NoReturn calls to compute reachability.

explanation: A call to a function annotated `NoReturn` (or `Never`) ends the code path, so mypy marks the `print` as `Statement is unreachable` when `--warn-unreachable` is on. Without the flag nothing is reported, and code after the call is simply skipped by the checker. This is how `sys.exit` and `assert_never` integrate with narrowing.

Python 3.13 adds `ReadOnly` for TypedDict keys. Which line does mypy reject?

```python
from typing import TypedDict, ReadOnly

class Profile(TypedDict):
    id: ReadOnly[int]
    name: str

p: Profile = {"id": 1, "name": "Ada"}   # line 1
p["name"] = "Grace"                     # line 2
p["id"] = 2                             # line 3
```

options.text: Line 3 only
options.why: A ReadOnly key can be set at creation but not assigned later.

options.text: Line 1, because a ReadOnly key cannot be set in a literal
options.why: Providing the key when creating the dict is allowed.

options.text: Lines 2 and 3, because one ReadOnly key freezes the whole dict
options.why: Only the marked key is read-only; `name` stays writable.

options.text: None, because ReadOnly is only checked at runtime
options.why: It is a static-only marker; Python itself never blocks the write.

explanation: `ReadOnly[...]` (PEP 705) marks a key that may be set when the dict is created but not mutated afterwards, so mypy reports `ReadOnly TypedDict key "id" TypedDict is mutated` on line 3. Creating the dict with the key is fine, and other keys stay writable. As with all TypedDict rules, nothing stops the write at runtime.

mypy runs with `--warn-unused-ignores` on this line:

```python
z: int = "s"  # type: ignore[arg-type]
```

Which does it report? (Choose two.)

options.text: An `[assignment]` error for the incompatible value
options.why: The listed code doesn't match, so the real error is not silenced.

options.text: An `[unused-ignore]` error for the comment
options.why: No `arg-type` error exists on the line, so the ignore is unused.

options.text: Nothing, since any `type: ignore` comment silences the line
options.why: Only a bare `# type: ignore` silences everything; codes narrow it.

options.text: An `[arg-type]` error, since that code was named
options.why: Naming a code silences it; it does not create it.

options.text: A syntax error, since codes must be listed in parentheses
options.why: Square brackets are the correct syntax.

explanation: The scoped ignore lists `arg-type`, but the actual error is `assignment`, so the error still surfaces and the ignore is flagged as unused. mypy also adds a note explaining that `assignment` is not covered by the comment. Fix it by naming the right code: `# type: ignore[assignment]`.

options.text: An error: no base class defines a `runn` to override
options.why: The decorator turns a misspelt override into a type error.

options.text: No error: `@override` only matters at runtime
options.why: Its main job is the static check; at runtime it merely sets a flag.

options.text: An error: `B` must also override `run`
options.why: Overriding is never mandatory for non-abstract methods.

options.text: No error, unless `A.run` is marked `@final`
options.why: `@final` would block overriding `run`; it is unrelated to the typo.

explanation: `@override` (PEP 698, Python 3.12) declares that a method must override something in a base class. Because of the typo, `runn` overrides nothing and mypy reports `Method "runn" is marked as an override, but no base method was found with this name`. Without the decorator the typo would silently create a new method. At runtime `@override` only sets `__override__ = True`.

stem: Python 3.12 added the `type` statement. Given `type Alias = list[int]`, which statements are true at runtime? (Choose two.)

options.text: `type(Alias)` is `typing.TypeAliasType`
options.why: The statement creates a TypeAliasType object.

options.text: `type Lazy = list[Undefined]` raises nothing until `Lazy.__value__` is read
options.why: The alias value is evaluated lazily.

options.text: `isinstance([], Alias)` returns `True`
options.why: TypeAliasType is not a class, so isinstance raises TypeError.

options.text: `Alias is list[int]` is `True`
options.why: The alias wraps the value; it is a different object.

options.text: Reassigning `Alias = str` afterwards is a `SyntaxError`
options.why: It is an ordinary name binding; Python allows rebinding it.

explanation: `type Alias = ...` creates a `typing.TypeAliasType` whose value is evaluated lazily, on first access to `__value__`. So `type Lazy = list[Undefined]` defines fine and only raises `NameError` when `__value__` is read. A `TypeAliasType` is not a class, so `isinstance([], Alias)` raises `TypeError`, and `Alias` is a distinct object from `list[int]`.
